samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Austin Tiso was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: Interview with Mr. John Austin Tiso, U.S. Navy Seabee. Date of Birth: September 28,1926. He served in World War II, Korea and the U.S. Naval Reserves. He achieved the rank of E-9. Interview was conducted on March 8, 2011,at V.A. Hudson Valley Health Care Castle Point Campus, Castle Point, New York. Interview was conducted by Mr. Tiso's daughter Ann Coschigano and Hospital Volunteer Eileen M. Fontanella. This interview is being conducted for the Veterans History Project in the American Folklife Center at the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Oh, what am I going to tell them first, about how I enlisted?

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: That you got in... She has the fact that you enlisted, so what happened once you got in the service...Where did you go?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Where I went, yeah. When I enlisted into the service, in the Seabees of the U.S. Navy, I took my boot training in Norfolk, Virginia. While I was there, I celebrated my fifteenth birthday in boot camp, in Norfolk, Virginia...after messing up my date of birth and what-have-you...right...in the meantime, I went to try to enlist into the Navy...because my wife, I'm sorry, my mother and my father. My father was working on the Pentagon, doing the fancy work on the Pentagon, and he would come home every two weeks, but my mom was home because there were ....six boys that she raised. I was the youngest. I enlisted. The others all were drafted into the infantry in the United States Army. I was the first one to go in, even though I was the youngest. I enlisted. My other brothers were all drafted. They were all drafted into the infantry, though, lucky for me...I found out later it was very, very good for me...so anyway, what had happened, after they checked it out, checked out all the paperwork, the recruiter says, "This has been changed." I said, "No it hasn't." [Recruiter replies] "Well, if it has not been changed," he says, "you better come back with an original...an original baptismal paper or birth certificate. The birth certificate has been altered, and the color has come out..." Today, if you did it today, you could do it ...[not clear] Yeah, so, this is what happened.

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: So then you went to...

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: So I went to a friend of mine, who was an altar boy...here's where the mischief comes in...he was an altar boy in the church that I go to...that we went to...I said, "Oh, I'm in a lot of trouble!" I said, "...Nicky, I'm in an awful lot of trouble!" [Friend replies] "What did you do now?" [John replies] "I went and joined the Navy, tried to join the Navy, and I changed my birth certificate...and they found out that I changed my birth certificate. You better come back with an original birth certificate...and you better come back because you're in a lot of trouble." I said," OK...what am I going to do now!" Like I said before, my dad was working on the Pentagon, and he was not home. My mom was home, she had to take care of the six boys....I said, "Ma, you know I hate school." She said, "No, you hate school! You never liked to go to school..." That's how she raised her boys, they never liked ...school! I says, "But I got a way out." [Mom replies] "What do you mean, you got a way out?" "You sign these papers...and they say, the Navy is gonna send me to school!"...I said, "Oh yeah, " ...she says, "Yeah..." [John] "But Ma, you better sign the papers!" [Mom says] "To go to school?...[John] Yeah, the Navy's gonna send me to school." So she said, "Bring the papers to me." So I brought the papers to her...and at the bottom of the paper that she signed, you got to bring it to the notary, to have it notarized.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So you did?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah...So, I knew the guy at the stationery store, right? And, when I went there...[John said] "You got to notarize these papers for me," I said, "Sal,"...his name was Sal, too... "you got to notarize these papers." [Sal replies] "Where's your mother?" [John replies] "Oh, she's at home, the kids will be coming home from school pretty soon for their lunch...so, you got to notarize this for me, and you know the family." [Sal replies] "OK." So he notarized them, OK. I brought it back. I says, "Oh!" I went back with the papers. He [the recruiter] says," Oh, you would have been in a lot of trouble if you didn't show up with these...papers/

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: But, they accepted them?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah...OK, so then I said, "Well, OK, these papers are all right...but [recruiter must have said] "All you need is your mother's signature...I know your father's in Washington, and he's not home to do it for you, but I'm sure your mother will sign for it after you tell them what you had to do. So that's what I did." (This is a slight repetition...So I went there and I said, "Sal you got to notarize this," I know that I'm repeating myself, but... "you got to notarize this!" He says, "Yeah, OK, but ...when will your mother come with you?" I just repeated...I said, "The kids are in school..'.)

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So then what was your next step after they accepted you?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: After they accepted me, they swore me in.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Right there?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: No, I had to go back down to 90 Church Street. I had to go back to 90 Church Street.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: In New York City?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: In New York City, and that's where I was sworn in.... on top of that to have so many people to get in because it was a few months after Pearl Harbor, and the lines were veiy, very long to get in to the service. A lot of them there were afraid they were going to be drafted, so they went down to enlist. That's what they did.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So once you were sworn in, ( Mr. Tiso : Yeah) what happened after that?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Once I was sworn in, they said it's gonna to be about three or four months before you'd be called because the back up, we had a lot of people that wanted to come into the service...whether they want the Marine Corps, Army or the Navy. Right?... but you have to wait because the line is long. I said OK, you know, that's all right, yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So they called you in three months?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Before that, because I...So I called the Navy Department I said ...what a long piece of time to get into the Navy...I got to wait three or four months before I can be sworn in? So I called my Congressman...what the hell is his name? Cunningham? I can't even think of his name, the Congressman...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: But you got hold of him?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I called...not him, I got a hold of his secretary, and I told 'em what happened. I said, "They won't accept me for three months." I says," You know, in three months this war might be over....I'd rather go in now! I want to go in now! I don't want to go out and get in trouble, I want to go in the Navy now!" Two days later I get a letter from the Congressman: Report to 90 Church St., and you will be sworn into the Navy...as soon as you get this paper. You go down there with the paper, and you give it to somebody...he gave me the name of the person who was a commander. And he says, "OK,"... he looked at every thing...[the commander] "The papers are all in place...we will now swear you in." They swore me in right then and there.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So once you're sworn in, then what happened?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Then after I was sworn in, they said you gotta wait before you go on active duty. I said, "I don't wanna wait, I want to go in now! I want to go in now!" "OK," he says, "...we'll take you now, but you're still going to have to wait...[until] after we swear you in."

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Where was the first place they sent you?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: The first place that they sent me was 90 Church St. (not clear...).

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: After that?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: After that I went to Norfolk, Virginia. Interviewer Ann (Mr. Tiso's Daughter): OK. And how long was the boot camp?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Boot camp, I'm trying to think was five weeks in boot camp? So, after boot camp...here's a thing that could be very funny: My dad had a tattoo, OK? And I remember him....he got a pumice stone....and, he, my dad, he used to try to take his tattoo off, OK? The tattoo was only seventy-five cents. In them days, seventy-five cents! Can you believe it? Now you can't even get...(laughter)...The three of us at the boot camp, the three of us went to town....to have a tattoo... Interviewers: To get a tattoo?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: To get a tattoo...the three of us. So we all had the Seabee and the anchor, U.S. Navy, stenciled on at the...[tattoo parlor] ...and then, I said, "You guys can go first...seventy-five cents...you know." So...what comes to my mind, I'm seeing my father trying to take his tattoos off-

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: You're thinking about it in your brain?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeah...[Not clear] What the heck was it, he was a first World War [veteran]....and the stories he used to tell us, you know...and he became a citizen in 1905, OK? So then, he did all that...I go into town, the three of us, right?

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: And you're sitting there?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, and I sat there...for seventy-five cents they put a stencil on it to outline the tattoo, right? All of a sudden, in my brain, I'm seeing my dad trying to get his off...trying to get his off, right...when I saw that, I says, "Here, here's the seventy-five cents." He already stenciled it...I says...He says, "I already stenciled it...I'm ready to go!" I said, "No! Here, take the seventy-five cents!"

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So you got out of there?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: I got out of there...Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Never got a tattoo?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Never got a tattoo...but my kids are not like me...

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: Well, his boys are, his other daughter, too...

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah...You know...So that's what happened there.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So then after you got your tat...got away from your tattoo, I should say...Did you stay in that area or were they transferring you out of there? What did you do? Mr. Tiso speaks of the sinking of the Henry R. Mallory, a ship used to transport soldiers to Europe

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: ...When they transferred me, I went to Iceland, OK...and the ship a hundred miles off the coast of Iceland was torpedoed.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: What was the ship?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: The Henry R. Mallory...it was a banana boat...I always call it, but they used it, you know,to take the troops over, and that's how we got there ....and that battalion were all saved because the regular Merchants (Merchant Marine) on there stand by and they saw that we all got off. They weren't saved. (

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: They weren't?) ....a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: What time of year were you there? Was it cold?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: December.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: That had to be pretty difficult.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, it was in December.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Were you in a convoy?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah, we went over in a convoy. [Slight interruption)

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: What did they call it?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Coffin Corner.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: And that was Iceland?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Iceland...

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: And that's because that's where all the torpedoes were?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: The torpedoes came and they sunk a lot of...ships on the convoy. That's what they called itâ€”convoy...and Coffin Corner, that's how it got Coffin Corner.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: What was your position?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: In the service?

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: When you were on the boat, when you were in Iceland?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: When I was in Iceland, I was on heavy equipment. I was doing ...changing the oil on all the heavy equipment. Seabees are a construction battalion, OK? It was very, very cold, like I said, right? And what had happened, I used to come in all dirty, after being in, you know with the heavy equipment and so on. And one day, the guy who was in charge of the galley or the kitchen or the butcher shop, he said, "Tiso, we're gonna take you out of the field...and you're going to become, we're going to teach you the meat business."

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: To what? Meat business. Oh, Meat business...OK.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: They learned me how to be a meat cutter, OK? And, that's what I did. They didn't want to see me outside, they knew how old I was, OK? And they really went out of their way...They said, He's only a kid... we had to ... had to look out for him, you know? And....after...they says, "Hey Tis, how about singing a song for us?" Yeah...I...yeah...

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: He used to sing a lot...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So, what did you sing?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Well, that.... "I'm Dreaming of a White Christmas." I'll never forget, it was a very ....on the way to Iceland...in December...and everybody was around the deck, downstairs, in the lobby...and, I'm singing ....I'm dreaming of a white Christmas, just like the ones I used to know...where the treetops glisten and children listen, to hear sleigh bells in the snow...I'm dreaming of a white Christmas, with every Christmas card I write...may your days be snowy and bright, and may all your Christmases be white.. [Laughter...and he talks about singing a little... and a career in singing]

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Forget about it..

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: You'll never make any money that way

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: No! Because you know who's after them? You gotta start out with the mafia.

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: He's trying to think about which one [story] to tell you.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, but the thing was twenty five years ago [Ann: It was longer than that, Daddy] ...Oh, it was longer than that, yes, yes...[Ann says: You've got a daughter who's sixty-one.] ....it was, it was in ...no, no...

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: It was seventy years ago, at least

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, but that's what I'm trying to think of the year...the Henry R. Mallory...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: How ...in 1942...wasn't that when there was a lot going on in Iceland, 1942 ...1943?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, but that was in Normandy, Omaha Beach, in France, yeah.....and my best buddy was standing next to me, and he got hit with an Eighty-eight and died just like that. Standing next to me, and that's why I got it in the leg.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: On the beach? Were you on the beach?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, on the beach, yeah, we were going on to the beach, and he was standing right next to me, and I felt very, very bad...my Jimmy, who was my buddy. When we were in England and Scotland...he came to America when he was four or five years old, OK, and he joined the Navy. And, he said, "You want to come and see my grandparents?" I says, "Yeah, let's go." Well, from Ireland, we went to Scotland. He said, "Let's look up my grandparents." So you want to know something...he came here when he was four or five years old, right....when he came... and they says, "Oh!" They recognized him! Now remember, four or five years old...and he's up there, right...And she said, "Want to go see your Grandpa? He's down at the shipyard, working down at the shipyard"...I said, "Yeah, is he locally?" [She said] "Yeah, he's only down the street, they're building the ships..." ...Can you believe? What I want to bring out, he was only four or five years old when he came to America.

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: And they hadn't seen him in all those years?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: And they hadn't seen him in so many years...and he saw him, and they both went toward each other...They recognized each other [not clear....] And, yeah, and he said, he said, "We'll go home, go to the house, I'll be getting off...I'm gonna ask to get off earlier today so I can spend some time with you." So, that's what we did. And then, when he got killed, I couldn't bring it to myself to go back again, but I did after the war, after the war, yeah...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: And you found the grandparents?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, no, I saw the house, I went into the house... they treated me very well, and uh, but uh, I just couldn't bring myself....but I had to tell them, finally I had to tell them...cause... that as far as I know, he had no pain ....cause it was very quick. The Eighty-eight killed him and put the shrapnel all up and down my...they got every thing but on my right leg. And whenever my wife...we used to go on a flight...she would never go overseas, but whenever we went to Florida or something, she says, "Here we go again!" We had to go through the [metal detectors], right... But, before I went I had the letter and I said [not clear]... he said, "Whenever you come, just pull over to the side..." It was something. A lot of good things happened Note: Mr. Tiso, who was fourteen when he enlisted, mentions that he belongs to an organization of veterans who were underage when they joined the military to serve in World War II. He takes out his membership card to show the interviewers.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: ....To say how many people were underage...and they call it Veterans of Underage...Do I have my card here? Call it Veterans of Underage Military Service...[looking for the card...] Maybe it's on that side, honey? Yeah, there it is. It's right on the top, I believe...No, no...[Ann: Right there...this one] That's it.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Veterans of Underage Military Service, Life Member. q I didn't know that this even exists.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: The youngest one ... twelve years old!

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Is that right! I can't imagine...

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, right...Not today, anyway, twelve years old? They all... from down south, you know... Mr. Tiso's recollections of landing in Normandy to prepare the beach for the soldiers who were to follow.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: OK. I landed on the beach in Normandy, in part of France...and it's Omaha Beach. It was the worst beach to land on, and my company was the first one to land ...and make everything safe for the people that were coming in after me, or after us.

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: What did you have to do when you landed?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: When we landed we had to get rid of all the obstacles in the way... they had wire, they had barbed wire and stuff like that...You had to be there, you had to cut them with bolt cutters. And that's what my job was there...and...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: You went into the water with the wire cutters?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Right on the edge of the beach...so that the other people that had to come in did not get tangled up...in the barbed wire...right.

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: Didn't you tell me you had to...you built the places where they stayed and stuff...?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: We built the concrete docks. They were invented by [not clear]......and they brought them over ... they were made of out of concrete...and they would float them over to make a breakwater, or a bridge. And that was our job.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: To put those together?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, to put them together, right. 1ft

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: You had to have a lot of teamwork to do that?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Right, yeah, yeah.... I was only a sixteen year old boy. Mr. Tiso talks about working in the kitchens, horsemeat provided for the guard dogs, and having the Galley at Camp Smith in Peekskill, New York, named the Chief Tiso Galley

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: And then you started working in the kitchen, and you became a cook.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeah...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: What did that involve, when you were a cook? How many [people] did you cook for?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: How many? Oh, a whole battalion...it was about twenty-eight people...about twenty-eight...it's the whole thing, it's the whole battalion.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: And this was on the boat?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: No, no. This was on the land.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: ...So what did you cook?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Whatever was on the menu...we got the frozen stuff in, to take it out the night before, or the day before so it thawed out, and then we would make sure it was thawed out, and then we had a night shift on that would come and cook it... You're gonna love this: After we made the Keflavik airport they transferred us again to another part of Iceland. And we went there, we hear people screaming...our own people....they [thought] it was horsemeat! I told that story? [

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: No, but I have heard that before...]

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, yeahL.Not for us...they had canine dogs. They had guard dogs, and the horsemeat was for the guard dogs. But we didn't know....You know? [Not clear]

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: I have heard that, that they made soup out of different kinds of things like that ...Did you like that? Did you like being a cook?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah, I liked it. I learned a lot...and...

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: He went on in the Reserves. He was the main cook ...at Camp Smith (in Peekskill, New York)...

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: They named the galley after me.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: They did? Interviewer Ann and

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah....they had a big party for him, and they named the galley after him.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: So it's called the Tiso Galley?

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: Chief Tiso

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Chief Tiso!

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Yeah...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: And it's still there?

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: And this is at Camp Smith down in Peekskill?

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: You know where that is, right?

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: I do. My husband trained there.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: My husband was in the Air Force

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: OK. Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: He was in the Reserves and he got called up.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Right

sp.speaker: Ann Coschigano
sp.p: (Ann explains that Mr. Tiso was designated Master Chief) Master Chief.

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: Master Chief, as in?

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Master Chief...

sp.speaker: Eileen Fontanella
sp.p: OK. You have had this experience, what have you come away from it with, and you said you don't recommend that people fight.

sp.speaker: John Austin Tiso
sp.p: Right. Conclusion: A few weeks after the taped interview, we asked again about the lessons that Mr. Tiso learned from this experience in the military. He summed it up concisely by saying: "What did I learn? Always be sure of what is going on and hope you're going to be all right." He also said that he learned to operate heavy equipment, and he added with a chuckle: "I learned to cut meat!" Mr. Tiso also mentioned that part of the Navy Seabees' job in Iceland was to build Meeks Field, the Keflavik airport. He believes it was one of the best airports the military built. The Seabees were a specialized arm of the U.S. Navy. They served as a newly formed construction battalion with the advent of the United States' participation in World War II. They assumed the job of building Meeks Field to allow for stopovers of military transatlantic flights and special handling of heavy bombers. Ann, Mr. Tiso's daughter, said that Mr. Tiso talked often of singing in different places. He sang for the USO Club when he was in England. Just a few days ago this interviewer and Ann attended a party on the unit where Mr. Tiso is in residence. He sang "Oh Danny Boy" and "When Irish Eyes are Smiling" for the residents and staff on the unit. His voice is extraordinary. It was a moment that was profoundly moving for everyone there.
